evidence: CatalogueModule.ts: createCatalogueUseCases builds AddProductUseCase, ListCatalogueUseCase and ListStockLevelsUseCase from deps.products, so all three share one repository dependency.
AddProductUseCase.ts and ListStockLevelsUseCase.ts both call toStockLevelDto from ProductMapper.ts. ListCatalogueUseCase.ts calls toCatalogueItemDto. No use case builds a DTO inline.
ProductMapper.ts: toCatalogueItemDto and toStockLevelDto both take availability from product.available, so it is never recomputed from onHand and reserved.
ProductDtos.ts is the only place AddProductCommand, CatalogueItemDto and StockLevelDto are defined.
productCommandParsers.ts: parseAddProductCommand builds AddProductCommand using the shared requireRecord, requireString and requireInteger guards.
AddProductUseCase.ts: the duplicate-id check (findById, then ConflictError) exists only here.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: The module passes: all seven files deal with one concern, the product catalogue. CatalogueModule.ts wires the three use cases from a single ProductRepository dependency. Each use case (AddProductUseCase, ListCatalogueUseCase, ListStockLevelsUseCase) puts an interface in front of its class, all in the same way. All three use cases build their output through the shared mappers in ProductMapper.ts instead of assembling DTOs themselves. The DTO shapes live only in ProductDtos.ts. Each rule sits in one place: availability always comes from the domain's product.available in both mappers, and is never recomputed from onHand minus reserved. Checking for an existing product id happens only in AddProductUseCase. Input parsing for AddProductCommand happens only in productCommandParsers.ts, which reuses the shared inputGuards helpers. I found no unrelated concerns, no duplicated rules and no files going around the module's own abstractions.
